Momentum Stability and Adaptive Control in Stochastic Reconfiguration

Yuyang Wang ††thanks: State Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences , Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China and School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China (email: wangyuyang@lsec.cc.ac.cn).    Xin Liu ††thanks: State Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China and School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China (e-mail: liuxin@lsec.cc.ac.cn).
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) combined with expressive neural network wavefunctions has become a powerful route to high-accuracy ground-state calculations, yet its practical success hinges on efficient and stable wavefunction optimization. While stochastic reconfiguration (SR) provides a geometry-aware preconditioner motivated by imaginary-time evolution, its Kaczmarz-inspired variant, subsampled projected-increment natural gradient descent (SPRING), achieves state-of-the-art empirical performance. However, the effectiveness of SPRING is highly sensitive to the choice of a momentum-like parameter μ\mu. The original sensitivity of μ\mu and the instability observed at μ=1\mu=1, have remained unclear. In this work, we clarify the distinct mechanisms governing the regimes μ<1\mu<1 and μ=1\mu=1. We establish convergence guarantees for 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1 under mild assumptions, and construct counterexamples showing that μ=1\mu=1 can induce divergence via uncontrolled growth along kernel-related directions when the step-size is not summable. Motivated by these theoretical insights and numerical observations, we further propose Principal Range Informed MomEntum SR (PRIME-SR), a tuning-free momentum-adaptive SR method based on effective spectral dimension and subspace overlap. PRIME-SR achieves performance comparable to optimally tuned SPRING while significantly improving robustness in VMC optimization.

1 Introduction

Computing the ground-state of a quantum many-body system is a fundamental problem in computational physics, materials science, and quantum chemistry. Such a system is governed by a self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator ℋ\mathscr{H}, and the goal is to determine its lowest eigenvalue EGSE_{\text{GS}} called ground-state energy, and the associated eigenfunction ψGS\psi_{\text{GS}} called ground-state wavefunction,

ℋψGS=EGSψGS,ψGS∈ℱ:={ψ:ΩN→ℂ,ψ≠0 satisfies certain physical symmetry.}\mathscr{H}\psi_{\text{GS}}=E_{\text{GS}}\psi_{\text{GS}},\qquad\psi_{\text{GS}}\in\mathcal{F}:=\{\psi:\Omega^{N}\to\mathbb{C},\psi\neq 0\text{ satisfies certain physical symmetry.}\}

where NN denotes the number of particles and Ω\Omega is the single-particle configuration space. In realistic settings, accurately approximating ground-state remains challenging due to the curse of dimensionality, the strong correlations encoded in ℋ\mathscr{H}, and additional physical constraints that generally prevent ψ\psi from factorizing [36].

Variational methods based on the Rayleigh-Ritz principle provide a flexible route to this problem by recasting the eigenvalue computation as minimization of the energy functional

EGS=infψ∈ℱ⟨ψ|ℋ|ψ⟩⟨ψ|ψ⟩.E_{\text{GS}}=\inf_{\psi\in\mathcal{F}}\dfrac{\braket{\psi|\mathscr{H}|\psi}}{\braket{\psi|\psi}}.

From this viewpoint, Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [24, 9] considers a parametrized family of trial wavefunctions ψ𝜽\psi_{\bm{\theta}} with 𝜽∈ℝNp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}} and turns the optimization over wavefunctions into an optimization over parameters in ℝNp\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}. By rewriting the objective as an expectation and estimating it using Monte Carlo sampling, VMC evaluates high-dimensional expectation values without explicitly representing ψ𝜽\psi_{\bm{\theta}} over the full configuration space (see Section 2.1 for details). This feature enables VMC to handle system sizes far beyond those accessible to deterministic discretization-based methods such as configuration interaction [29] and multi-configuration self-consistent field [14].

In recent years, neural networks have substantially increased the expressiveness of trial wavefunctions. Following the seminal work of Carleo and Troyer [6], a broad class of neural network-based and physics-inspired wavefunctions has been developed [27, 12, 35, 18, 42], together with theoretical studies of their representational capability [2, 39, 36]. These advances have substantially enhanced the approximation power of wavefunctions, thereby enabling near-exact ground-state energy computations in both electronic-structure and lattice settings [13], and opening the era of neural network-based VMC (NN-VMC).

Despite these successes, optimizing neural network wavefunctions remains challenging [37]. Standard optimizers in deep learning such as Adam [16] and AdamW [22] often perform poorly in this context because of the complex landscape of neural network wavefunctions [27, 35]. In practice, a variety of optimization methods based on the geometry and physics of VMC have been developed. These include stochastic reconfiguration (SR) and related natural gradient methods [27, 30, 31, 32], variants of the linear method [33, 40, 38], and more recent manifold-based approaches [25, 3, 17]. While these methods have demonstrated strong empirical performance, many of them require solving large linear systems whose size scales with the number of model parameters NpN_{p}, resulting in a per-iteration computational cost of 𝒪⁡(Np3)\mathcal{O}(N_{p}^{3}) and consequently limiting their scalability.

Among these approaches, SR-based methods are the most widely used in large scale NN-VMC applications (see Section 2.2 for a detailed introduction to SR). In contrast to linear method and manifold-based approaches, which often require additional backpropagation steps or lack effective cost-reduction structures, SR admits a natural reformulation that enables scalable approximations [23, 27, 7, 10, 28, 41, 11]. This has motivated a range of scalable SR variants that approximate or reformulate the SR update in a computationally tractable way for large neural network wavefunctions.

Existing scalable SR methods can be broadly categorized by the approximation viewpoint they adopt. Structure exploiting approaches approximate the SR matrix using block-diagonal and Kronecker-factorized forms, leading to K-FAC-type methods [23, 27]. Low-rank approaches exploit the intrinsic rank deficiency of the SR matrix, for instance via truncated or warm-started singular value decomposition (SVD) techniques [41]. Finally, least-squares-based approaches interpret the SR update as an underdetermined linear system and select specific solutions, such as Minimum-step SR (MinSR) [7, 28] and the Subsampled Projected-Increment Natural Gradient (SPRING) method [10]. Notably, these least-squares formulations allow the use of the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, reducing the per-iteration cost to nearly linear in the number of parameters.

Among these SR variants, SPRING has attracted particular attention due to its empirical state-of-the-art performance in NN-VMC [10, 11]. Motivated by randomized Kaczmarz projection methods [15, 8], SPRING reuses the previous update direction by projecting it onto the subspace identified by the current batch of samples, and then combines this projected direction with the current gradient information to form the next update (see Section 2.3 for details).

However, a central practical issue is that the stability and performance of SPRING depend critically on how strongly the previous direction is reused. The original work [10] reported that naively using the projected previous direction can lead to unstable optimization trajectories. To control the contribution of historical information, SPRING introduces a parameter μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) that weights the projected previous update direction. Although μ=1\mu=1 can lead to severe instability or even divergence, empirically, values of μ\mu close to 1 often accelerate convergence. Moreover, SPRING can be highly sensitive to μ\mu: a value that performs well on one problem may perform poorly on another, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (see Section 5 for experimental details). These observations motivate the two main goals of this paper: (i) to understand the mechanisms distinguishing the regimes μ<1\mu<1 and μ=1\mu=1, and (ii) to develop a principled momentum-adaptive SR method that avoids manual tuning while retaining the practical benefits of momentum reuse.

Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. (1)

    Convergence guarantees for SPRING with 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1. We establish convergence of noiseless SPRING to a first-order stationary point. In the stochastic setting with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Monte Carlo samples, we show that the expected norm of the gradient converges to zero up to a sampling error.

  2. (2)

    Divergence counterexamples for SPRING with μ=1\mu=1. Exploiting the fact that the VMC gradient lies in the range of the SR matrix, we construct explicit counterexamples showing that SPRING with μ=1\mu=1 can exhibit uncontrolled growth along kernel-related directions when the step-size is not summable, while the same constructions remain convergent for 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1.

  3. (3)

    PRIME-SR: a tuning-free momentum-adaptive SR method. Motivated by the theoretical insights and numerical observations, we propose Principal Range Informed MomEntum SR (PRIME-SR), a new SR variant that adaptively controls momentum reuse through effective spectral dimension and subspace overlap indicators derived from the SR matrix. PRIME-SR achieves performance comparable to optimally tuned SPRING. In particular, in electronic-structure problems where SPRING is sensitive to initialization and can be unstable, PRIME-SR remains consistently stable across different initializations.

Organization. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the VMC framework, SR, and the SPRING algorithm. In Section 3, we present the theoretical analysis of SPRING, including convergence results for 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1 and divergence mechanisms at μ=1\mu=1. In Section 4, we introduce PRIME-SR, a momentum-adaptive SR method motivated by kernel-range decompositions and numerical observations. In Section 5, we report numerical results on lattice spin systems as well as atomic and molecular systems. Finally, in Section 6, we summarize our findings and discuss future directions.

Notations. Throughout this paper, ℝ\mathbb{R} and ℂ\mathbb{C} denote the real and complex number fields, and 𝐢\mathbf{i} denotes the imaginary unit. Bold letters (e.g., 𝒙\bm{x}) represent vectors. The configuration space of particles is denoted by Ω\Omega, and ΩN\Omega^{N} denotes the NN-fold Cartesian product of Ω\Omega. We write 𝐱∈ΩN\mathbf{x}\in\Omega^{N} for particle configuration and 𝒙∈Ω\bm{x}\in\Omega for a single-particle configuration. The Hamiltonian is denoted by ℋ\mathscr{H}, the wavefunction by ψ\psi, and the parameters of a parameterized wavefunction by 𝜽\bm{\theta}. The symbol 𝟏\mathbf{1} denotes the all-ones vector of appropriate dimension, and σx\sigma^{x}, σy\sigma^{y}, and σz\sigma^{z} denote the Pauli matrices. We use the standard asymptotic notation fk=Ω⁡(gk)f_{k}=\Omega(g_{k}) to mean that there exist constants c>0c>0 and k0≥0k_{0}\geq 0 such that fk≥c​gkf_{k}\geq c\,g_{k} for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}.

The inner product is written in Dirac notation ⟨⋅|⋅⟩\braket{\cdot|\cdot}: it corresponds to the ℒ2\mathcal{L}^{2} inner product in continuous settings and the ℓ2\ell^{2} inner product for discrete vectors. The norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the 22-norm unless stated otherwise (matrix spectral norm, vector Euclidean norm, and function ℒ2\mathcal{L}^{2} norm). We use 𝔼\mathbb{E} for expectation, “i.i.d.” for independent and identically distributed, and “a.s.” for almost surely. We use ℱk\mathscr{F}_{k} to denote a σ\sigma-algebra filtration for discrete iterations, and σ⁡(X)\sigma(X) for the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the random variable XX.

2 Background and Preliminaries

In this section, we briefly review the VMC framework, the SR method, and the SPRING algorithm. The exposition is intentionally concise and focuses on aspects that are directly relevant to the subsequent sections.

2.1 Variational Monte Carlo

Consider a quantum system of NN particles with configuration 𝐱=(𝒙1,…,𝒙N)∈ΩN\mathbf{x}=(\bm{x}_{1},\dots,\bm{x}_{N})\in\Omega^{N} and wavefunction ψ:ΩN→ℂ\psi:\Omega^{N}\to\mathbb{C}. Here Ω\Omega denotes the single-particle configuration space, which is either discrete (e.g., lattice spin systems) or continuous (e.g., electronic systems). The system is governed by a self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator ℋ\mathscr{H}, and the goal is to compute its ground-state energy and wavefunction. Moreover, for the class of Hamiltonians considered in this work, including the electronic Hamiltonian and the TFI and Heisenberg models (see Appendix D for details), the real part of a ground-state wavefunction is also a ground-state wavefunction. Therefore, unless stated otherwise, we restrict attention to real-valued wavefunctions of the form ψ:ΩN↦ℝ\psi:\Omega^{N}\mapsto\mathbb{R}.

By the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle, the ground-state energy can be written as

EGS=infψ∈ℱL⁡[ψ]:=⟨ψ|ℋ|ψ⟩⟨ψ|ψ⟩=∫ΩNψ⁡(𝐱)​⟨𝐱|ℋ|ψ⟩​𝑑𝐱∫ΩN|ψ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱,s. t. ​ψ​ satisfies certain constraints.E_{\text{GS}}=\inf_{\psi\in\mathcal{F}}L[\psi]:=\dfrac{\braket{\psi|\mathscr{H}|\psi}}{\braket{\psi|\psi}}=\dfrac{\int_{\Omega^{N}}\psi(\mathbf{x})\braket{\mathbf{x}|\mathscr{H}|\psi}\mathrm{\,d}\mathbf{x}}{\int_{\Omega^{N}}\left|\psi(\mathbf{x})\right|^{2}\mathrm{\,d}\mathbf{x}},\quad\text{s. t. }\psi\text{ satisfies certain constraints.} (2.1)

When the configuration space is discrete, the integral denotes summation over ΩN\Omega^{N}:

∫ΩN⋅d𝐱:=∑𝒙1∈Ω⋯∑𝒙N∈Ω⋅.\int_{\Omega^{N}}\cdot\mathrm{\,d}\mathbf{x}:=\sum_{\bm{x}_{1}\in\Omega}\cdots\sum_{\bm{x}_{N}\in\Omega}\cdot.

In VMC, one introduces a parametrized ansätz ψ𝜽:ΩN↦ℝ\psi_{\bm{\theta}}:\Omega^{N}\mapsto\mathbb{R} with parameters 𝜽∈ℝNp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}} satisfying ψ𝜽∈ℱ\psi_{\bm{\theta}}\in\mathcal{F}. The ground-state energy EGSE_{\text{GS}} is then approximated by solving

E~GS:=min𝜽∈ℝNp⁡L⁡(𝜽):=L⁡[ψ𝜽].\tilde{E}_{\text{GS}}:=\min_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}L(\bm{\theta}):=L[\psi_{\bm{\theta}}].

Since the physical constraints (e.g., antisymmetry) are typically enforced by the parameterization, E~GS\tilde{E}_{\text{GS}} provides an upper bound on the true ground-state energy, i.e., E~GS≥EGS\tilde{E}_{\text{GS}}\geq E_{\text{GS}}.

Direct evaluation of L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) involves high-dimensional integrals or exponentially large sums. In VMC, the objective can be rewritten as an expectation:

L(𝜽)=∫|ψ𝜽​(𝐱)|2∫|ψ𝜽|2​d​𝐱′⏟=:π𝜽​(𝐱)⋅⟨𝐱|ℋ|ψ𝜽⟩ψ𝜽​(𝐱)⏟=:Eloc​(𝜽,𝐱)d𝐱=𝔼X∼π𝜽[Eloc(𝜽;X)].L(\bm{\theta})=\int\underbrace{\dfrac{\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\right|^{2}}{\int\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}\right|^{2}\mathrm{\,d}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}}_{=:\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})}\cdot\underbrace{\dfrac{\braket{\mathbf{x}|\mathscr{H}|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}}}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})}}_{=:E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};\mathbf{x})}\mathrm{\,d}\mathbf{x}=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};X)\right].

Here π𝜽∝|ψ𝜽|2\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\propto\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}\right|^{2} is the probability distribution induced by the wavefunction: for continuous systems it is a probability density, while for discrete systems it is a probability mass function on ΩN\Omega^{N}. The quantity Eloc​(𝜽,𝐱)E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};\mathbf{x}) is called the local energy [4].

Remark 2.1.

For continuous systems, ℋ\mathscr{H} acts on functions and ⟨𝐱|ℋ|ψ⟩=ℋ​ψ​(𝐱)\braket{\mathbf{x}|\mathscr{H}|\psi}=\mathscr{H}\psi(\mathbf{x}). For discrete systems, ψ\psi can be viewed as a vector |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} indexed by ΩN\Omega^{N}, and ℋ\mathscr{H} is represented by a matrix, ⟨𝐱|ℋ|ψ⟩=∑𝐱′∈ΩNψ⁡(𝐱′)​⟨𝐱|ℋ|𝐱′⟩\braket{\mathbf{x}|\mathscr{H}|\psi}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\Omega^{N}}\psi(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\braket{\mathbf{x}|\mathscr{H}|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}, where ⟨𝐱|ℋ|𝐱′⟩\braket{\mathbf{x}|\mathscr{H}|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}} is the (𝐱,𝐱′)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})-th element of matrix ℋ\mathscr{H}. Although this sum formally runs over an exponentially large configuration space, many Hamiltonians of interest in this work, such as the TFI and Heisenberg models, are sparse. Consequently, only a small number of terms are nonzero, and the cost of evaluating the local energy is typically 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N).

Therefore, within the VMC framework, computing the ground-state reduces to the stochastic optimization problem

min𝜽∈ℝNp⁡L⁡(𝜽)=𝔼X∼π𝜽​[Eloc​(𝜽,X)].\min_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}L(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};X)\right]. (2.2)

Moreover, the gradient of L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) admits the expression [21],

g⁡(𝜽):=∇𝜽L​(𝜽)=2​𝔼X∼π𝜽​[E¯​(𝜽,X)​O​(𝜽,X)],g(\bm{\theta}):=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L(\bm{\theta})=2\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};X)O(\bm{\theta};X)\right], (2.3)

where

E¯​(𝜽,𝐱):=Eloc​(𝜽,𝐱)−L⁡(𝜽)∈ℝ,O⁡(𝜽,𝐱):=∇𝜽​log​|ψ𝜽​(𝐱)|−𝔼X∼π𝜽​[∇𝜽​log​|ψ𝜽​(X)|]∈ℝNp.\begin{split}\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};\mathbf{x})&:=E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};\mathbf{x})-L(\bm{\theta})\in\mathbb{R},\\ O(\bm{\theta};\mathbf{x})&:=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\right|-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(X)\right|\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}.\end{split} (2.4)

In practice, both L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) and g⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta}) are estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples [9]. Let NsN_{s} denote the sample size, and let ℬ:={X1,…,XNs}\mathcal{B}:=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{N_{s}}\} be a batch of samples. The standard Monte Carlo estimators of L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) and g⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta}) are

L⁡(𝜽)≈L⁡(𝜽,ℬ):=1Ns​∑i=1NsEloc​(𝜽,Xi)g⁡(𝜽)≈g⁡(𝜽,ℬ):=2Ns−1​∑i=1NsE¯​(𝜽,Xi,ℬ)​O​(𝜽,Xi,ℬ),\begin{split}L(\bm{\theta})&\approx L(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B}):=\dfrac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};X_{i})\\ g(\bm{\theta})&\approx g(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B}):=\dfrac{2}{N_{s}-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};X_{i},\mathcal{B})O(\bm{\theta};X_{i},\mathcal{B}),\end{split} (2.5)

where

E¯​(𝜽,Xi,ℬ):=Eloc​(𝜽,Xi)−L⁡(𝜽,ℬ),O⁡(𝜽,Xi,ℬ):=∇𝜽​log​|ψ𝜽​(Xi)|−1Ns​∑j=1Ns∇𝜽​log​|ψ𝜽​(Xj)|.\begin{split}\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};X_{i},\mathcal{B})&:=E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};X_{i})-L(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B}),\\ O(\bm{\theta};X_{i},\mathcal{B})&:=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(X_{i})\right|-\dfrac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(X_{j})\right|.\end{split} (2.6)

For a more compact representation, define

E¯​(𝜽,ℬ):=1Ns−1​(E¯​(𝜽,X1,ℬ),…,E¯​(𝜽,XNs,ℬ))⊤∈ℝNsO⁡(𝜽,ℬ):=1Ns−1​(O⁡(𝜽,X1,ℬ),…,O⁡(𝜽,XNs,ℬ))∈ℝNp×Ns.\begin{split}\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})&:=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}-1}}\left(\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};X_{1},\mathcal{B}),\dots,\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};X_{N_{s}},\mathcal{B})\right)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}}\\ O(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})&:=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}-1}}\left(O(\bm{\theta};X_{1},\mathcal{B}),\dots,O(\bm{\theta};X_{N_{s}},\mathcal{B})\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times N_{s}}.\end{split} (2.7)

Under these definitions, the gradient estimator can be written compactly as g⁡(𝜽,ℬ)=2​O​(𝜽,ℬ)​E¯​(𝜽,ℬ)g(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})=2O(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B}). Moreover, it is unbiased under i.i.d. sampling:

Lemma 2.1 ([1]).

Let ℬ:={X1,…,XNs}\mathcal{B}:=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{N_{s}}\} and X1,…,XNs∼i.i.dπ𝛉X_{1},\dots,X_{N_{s}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d}}}{{\sim}}\pi_{\bm{\theta}}. Then 𝔼ℬ​[g⁡(𝛉,ℬ)]=g⁡(𝛉)\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}}[g(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})]=g(\bm{\theta}).

2.2 Stochastic Reconfiguration

SR and its variants remain among the most widely used optimization methods in VMC, originally motivated by imaginary-time evolution [30, 31]. In essence, SR chooses the parameter update so that the variation of the parameterized wavefunction matches an infinitesimal imaginary-time evolution step (see [4] for details). The resulting SR update can be written as

𝜽k+1:=𝜽k+ηk​Δ​𝜽k,Δ​𝜽k∈arg⁡minΔ​𝜽∈ℝNp⁡Δ​𝜽⊤​S​(𝜽k)​Δ​𝜽+g​(𝜽k)⊤​Δ​𝜽,\begin{split}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}&:=\bm{\theta}_{k}+\eta_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k},\\ \Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}&\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{\Delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}~\Delta\bm{\theta}^{\top}S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\Delta\bm{\theta}+g(\bm{\theta}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta},\end{split}

where ηk\eta_{k} denotes the step-size, and S⁡(𝜽):=𝔼X∼π𝜽​[O⁡(𝜽,X)​O​(𝜽,X)⊤]∈RNp×NpS(\bm{\theta}):=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[O(\bm{\theta};X)O(\bm{\theta};X)^{\top}\right]\in R^{N_{p}\times N_{p}} is the SR matrix, which is also known as the Fisher information matrix [27]. Using the expression of g⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta}) in Eq. (2.3), the SR direction can equivalently be characterized as

Δ​𝜽k=arg⁡minΔ​𝜽∈ℝNp⁡𝔼X∼π𝜽k​[|O​(𝜽k,X)⊤​Δ​𝜽+E¯​(𝜽k,X)|2].\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\Delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}}\left[\left|O(\bm{\theta}_{k};X)^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}+\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};X)\right|^{2}\right]. (2.8)

In practice, let ℬk:={Xk,1,…,Xk,Ns}\mathcal{B}_{k}:=\{X_{k,1},\dots,X_{k,N_{s}}\} be the sample batch drawn from π𝜽k\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}. Using the notation in Eq. (2.7), the SR update becomes

𝜽k+1=𝜽k+ηk​Δ​𝜽k,Δ​𝜽k∈arg⁡minΔ​𝜽∈ℝNp⁡‖O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​Δ​𝜽+E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk)‖2.\begin{split}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}&=\bm{\theta}_{k}+\eta_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k},\\ \Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}&\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{\Delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}\left\|O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}+\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right\|^{2}.\end{split} (2.9)

Equivalently, Δ​𝜽k\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k} solves the linear least-squares system O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​Δ​𝜽=−E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk)O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}=-\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}) with NpN_{p} unknowns and NsN_{s} equations.

In the NN-VMC era, the number of parameters can be extremely large, and one typically has Np≫NsN_{p}\gg N_{s}. On the one hand, directly solving an NpN_{p}-dimensional linear system is impractical; on the other hand, Eq. (2.9) becomes an underdetermined least-squares problem with infinitely many solutions. In [7], the authors exploited this underdetermined structure and proposed selecting the minimum-norm solution, leading to the MinSR method whose update can be computed at cost 𝒪⁡(Ns3+Np​Ns2)\mathcal{O}(N_{s}^{3}+N_{p}N_{s}^{2}). It highlights the role of the underdetermined structure in large scale SR. This perspective also motivates the SPRING method.

2.3 SPRING

SPRING, introduced in [10], is a recent SR variant motivated by the randomized Kaczmarz method for overdetermined least-squares problems [15, 8]. Since the parameter 𝜽\bm{\theta} usually changes gradually, the SR equations often vary only mildly from one iteration to the next. Based on randomized Kaczmarz method, the SPRING uses the previous update direction as a reference and corrects it with the current SR system. This leads to the following projection-inspired update:

Δ​𝜽k:=arg⁡minΔ​𝜽∈ℝNp⁡‖Δ​𝜽−Δ​𝜽k−1‖2+1λ​‖O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​Δ​𝜽+E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk)‖2,\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}:=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\Delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\left\|O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}+\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right\|^{2}, (2.10)

where λ>0\lambda>0 is a regularization parameter.

However, as demonstrated in [10], the update in Eq. (2.10) can yield unstable optimization trajectories, and the origin of this instability was left unexplained. To improve stability, the authors introduced a decay factor, which is also called a momentum parameter, μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) applied to the previous update direction, resulting in the practical SPRING update

Δ​𝜽k:=arg⁡minΔ​𝜽∈ℝNp⁡‖Δ​𝜽−μ​Δ​𝜽k−1‖2+1λ​‖O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​Δ​𝜽+E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk)‖2=(λ​I+O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤)−1​(λ​μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk)).\begin{split}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}&:=\mathop{\arg\min}_{\Delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}-\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\left\|O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}+\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right\|^{2}\\ &=\left(\lambda I+O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\lambda\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right).\end{split} (2.11)

Using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, the computational cost of SPRING can be reduced to 𝒪⁡(Ns3+Ns2​Np)\mathcal{O}(N_{s}^{3}+N_{s}^{2}N_{p}), and the update can be written as

Δ​𝜽k=μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​(λ​I+O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​O​(𝜽k,ℬk))−1​ζk,\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\left(\lambda I+O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right)^{-1}\zeta_{k}, (2.12)

where

ζk:=μ​O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​Δ​𝜽k−1+E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk)∈ℝNs.\zeta_{k}:=\mu O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}+\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}}. (2.13)

To further stabilize the optimization, [10] introduced two additional techniques. The first addresses the potential singularity of O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​O​(𝜽k,ℬk)O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}) due to finite sampling. Let 𝟏∈ℝNs\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}} denote the all-ones vector. By the definition of O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}) in Eqs. (2.6) and (2.7), we have O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​𝟏=0O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\mathbf{1}=0. The authors proposed replacing Eq. (2.12) by

Δ​𝜽k=μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​(λ​I+O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​O​(𝜽k,ℬk)+1Ns​𝟏𝟏⊤)−1​ζk,\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\left(\lambda I+O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})+\frac{1}{N_{s}}\bm{1}\bm{1}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\zeta_{k}, (2.14)

since this modification does not change the update in exact arithmetic (see the derivation in [10]):

O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​(λ​I+O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​O​(𝜽k,ℬk)+1Ns​𝟏𝟏⊤)−1=O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)​(λ​I+O​(𝜽k,ℬk)⊤​O​(𝜽k,ℬk))−1.O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\left(\lambda I+O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})+\frac{1}{N_{s}}\bm{1}\bm{1}^{\top}\right)^{-1}=O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\left(\lambda I+O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})^{\top}O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right)^{-1}.

The second technique is a norm constraint inspired by K-FAC [23], which controls the update magnitude at each iteration,

𝜽k+1:=𝜽k+Δ​𝜽k⋅min⁡{ηk,C‖Δ​𝜽k‖},\bm{\theta}_{k+1}:=\bm{\theta}_{k}+\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\cdot\min\left\{\eta_{k},\frac{\sqrt{C}}{\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|}\right\}, (2.15)

where C>0C>0 is a prescribed constant. The resulting SPRING procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1.

3 Theoretical Analysis of SPRING

In this section, we develop a theoretical analysis of the SPRING iteration, with particular emphasis on the role of the momentum parameter μ\mu. We show that the regimes 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1 and μ=1\mu=1 exhibit fundamentally different behaviors, both theoretically and numerically.

We distinguish between two settings. First, we analyze a full-batch (deterministic) variant of SPRING, where the SR matrix and gradient are evaluated in expectation form. This setting allows us to isolate the intrinsic dynamics of the algorithm without stochastic effects. Second, we consider the practical stochastic setting induced by Monte Carlo sampling, where both the SR matrix and the gradient are estimated from finite samples.

Our main conclusions are as follows. When 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1, SPRING admits convergence guarantees under mild conditions. In contrast, when μ=1\mu=1, SPRING can diverge even in the full-batch setting, driven by an uncontrolled accumulation along kernel-related directions of the SR matrix.

Recall that the practical SPRING update can be written in compact form as

{𝜽k+1=𝜽k+ηk​Δ​𝜽k,Δ​𝜽k=(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k,ℬk))−1​(λ​μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−12​g​(𝜽k,ℬk)),\begin{cases}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}=\bm{\theta}_{k}+\eta_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k},\\ \Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right)^{-1}\left(\lambda\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-\dfrac{1}{2}g(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right),\end{cases} (SPRING)

and its full-batch counterpart is

{𝜽k+1=𝜽k+ηk​Δ​𝜽k,Δ​𝜽k=(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k))−1​(λ​μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−12​g​(𝜽k)).\begin{cases}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}=\bm{\theta}_{k}+\eta_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k},\\ \Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)^{-1}\left(\lambda\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-\dfrac{1}{2}g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right).\end{cases} (F-SPRING)
Remark 3.1.

The full-batch setting serves only as a noise-free baseline for analyzing the optimization behavior of SPRING. In this regime, all quantities are evaluated exactly over the full configuration space, so the residual error is not affected by Monte Carlo sampling noise. However, for lattice models, the deterministic cost grows exponentially with the system size, and exact evaluation is therefore feasible only for small systems. Hence, the full-batch setting is adopted here only for analysis and diagnostic comparison on small lattice models, and should not be regarded as a practical optimization setting.

3.1 Convergence Analysis of SPRING with 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1

We begin with the full-batch iteration (F-SPRING). This deterministic setting serves as a baseline for understanding SPRING and forms the foundation for the subsequent stochastic analysis.

We impose the following assumptions, which provide sufficient smoothness and moment control to carry out the convergence analysis.

Assumption 3.1.

The following hold:

  1. (1)

    There exists Cm>0C_{m}>0, such that for any 𝜽∈ℝNp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}},

    𝔼X∼π𝜽​[‖∇𝜽​log​|ψ𝜽​(X)|‖4]≤Cm,𝔼X∼π𝜽​[Eloc​(𝜽,X)4]≤Cm.\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\left|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(X)\right|\right\|^{4}\right]\leq C_{m},\quad\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{\theta};X)^{4}\right]\leq C_{m}.
  2. (2)

    The gradient g⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta}) is CgC_{g}-Lipschitz continuous, i.e., there exists Cg>0C_{g}>0, such that

    ‖g⁡(𝜽)−g⁡(𝜽′)‖≤Cg​‖𝜽−𝜽′‖,∀𝜽,𝜽′∈ℝNp.\left\|g(\bm{\theta})-g(\bm{\theta}^{\prime})\right\|\leq C_{g}\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\right\|,\quad\forall~\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}.
  3. (3)

    For any k≥0k\geq 0, the step-size ηk\eta_{k} satisfies

    0<ηk≤ηk−1,η0≤2​λ​(1−μ)Cg.0<\eta_{k}\leq\eta_{k-1},\quad\eta_{0}\leq\dfrac{2\lambda(1-\mu)}{C_{g}}.

The fourth-order moment bounds in Assumption 3.1 control higher-order fluctuations of the stochastic quantities and are standard in analyses of Monte Carlo estimators.

Remark 3.2.

We note that related moment bounds and smoothness have also appeared in the existing works that study the convergence of optimization methods for VMC, for example in the analysis of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [1]. In that work, Lipschitz continuity of the gradient is obtained by imposing additional regularity assumptions on second-order derivatives of ψ𝛉\psi_{\bm{\theta}}. Here, for simplicity and clarity, we directly assume Lipschitz continuity of g⁡(𝛉)g(\bm{\theta}), which is a common and convenient condition in optimization.

Lipschitz continuity of the gradient implies a quadratic upper bound for the objective L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}).

Lemma 3.1 ([26]).

If g⁡(𝛉)=∇𝛉L​(𝛉)g(\bm{\theta})=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L(\bm{\theta}) is CgC_{g}-Lipschitz continuous, then

L⁡(𝜽′)−L⁡(𝜽)≤g​(𝜽)⊤​(𝜽′−𝜽)+Cg2​‖𝜽′−𝜽‖2,∀𝜽,𝜽′∈ℝNp.L(\bm{\theta}^{\prime})-L(\bm{\theta})\leq g(\bm{\theta})^{\top}(\bm{\theta}^{\prime}-\bm{\theta})+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\left\|\bm{\theta}^{\prime}-\bm{\theta}\right\|^{2},\quad\forall~\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}.

Using this bound, we obtain the following convergence result for the full-batch SPRING iteration.

Theorem 3.1.

Under Assumption 3.1, let {𝛉k}\{\bm{\theta}_{k}\} be generated by (F-SPRING). Then for any 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1, there exist C>0C>0, such that, for any K≥1K\geq 1,

∑k=1Kηk​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2≤C.\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}\leq C.
Proof.

See Appendix A. ∎

Theorem 3.1 implies that, when 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1, the accumulated squared gradient norm is finite. As a direct consequence, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 3.1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.1:

  1. (1)

    If ∑kηk=∞\sum_{k}\eta_{k}=\infty, then

    min1≤k≤K⁡‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2=𝒪⁡(1∑k=1Kηk)andlim infk→∞‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖=0.\min_{1\leq k\leq K}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}=\mathcal{O}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\liminf_{k\to\infty}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|=0.
  2. (2)

    If ηk≡η>0\eta_{k}\equiv\eta>0, then limk→∞g⁡(𝜽k)=0\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}g(\bm{\theta}_{k})=0.

These results establish convergence to first-order stationary points in the deterministic setting. Notably, the restriction μ<1\mu<1 is essential: as μ→1\mu\to 1, the admissible step-size bound will vanish.

While Theorem 3.1 establishes convergence guarantees in the idealized full-batch setting, we now turn to the practical SPRING update with Monte Carlo sampling, given by (SPRING). In this setting, both the gradient and the SR matrix are estimated from finite samples, which introduces additional stochastic noise. To avoid complications arising from non-stationary Markov chains, we impose the following simplifying assumption on the sampled batches.

Assumption 3.2.

For k≥0k\geq 0, the sampled configurations ℬk:={Xk,i}i=1Ns\mathcal{B}_{k}:=\{X_{k,i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{s}} satisfy:

Xk,1,…,Xk,Ns∼i.i.d.π𝜽k.X_{k,1},\dots,X_{k,N_{s}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\pi_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}.

Under Assumption 3.2, Lemma 2.1 shows that the gradient estimator g⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)g(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}) is unbiased. The same assumption also implies that the SR matrix is an unbiased estimator of S⁡(𝜽k)S(\bm{\theta}_{k}).

Lemma 3.2.

Under Assumption 3.2, for any k≥0k\geq 0, 𝔼ℬk​[S⁡(𝛉k,ℬk)]=S⁡(𝛉k)\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}[S(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})]=S(\bm{\theta}_{k}).

Proof.

See Appendix B.1. ∎

Despite the unbiasedness of both g⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)g(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}) and S⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)S(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}), the SPRING update direction in (SPRING) is conditionally biased due to the matrix inversion. Specifically, conditioning on the σ\sigma-algebra generated by previous samples ℱk−1:=σ(Xi,j, 0≤i≤k−1, 1≤j≤Ns)\mathscr{F}_{k-1}:=\sigma\left(X_{i,j},\,0\leq i\leq k-1,\,1\leq j\leq N_{s}\right), we generally have

𝔼⁡[(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k,ℬk))−1​(λ​μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−12​g​(𝜽k,ℬk))|ℱk−1]≠(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k))−1​(λ​μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−12​g​(𝜽k)),\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right)^{-1}\left(\lambda\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-\dfrac{1}{2}g(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})\right)|\mathscr{F}_{k-1}\right]\neq\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)^{-1}\left(\lambda\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-\dfrac{1}{2}g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right),

This conditional bias introduces an additional error term in the convergence analysis and prevents convergence to an exact first-order stationary point.

Theorem 3.2.

Under Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, let {𝛉k}\{\bm{\theta}_{k}\} be generated by (SPRING). Then for any 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1, there exist C1,C2,C3>0C_{1},~C_{2},~C_{3}>0, such that, for any K≥1K\geq 1,

∑k=1Kηk​𝔼​[‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2]≤C1+C2​1Ns​∑k=1Kηk+C3​1Ns2​∑k=1Kηk.\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}\mathbb{E}[\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}]\leq C_{1}+C_{2}\dfrac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}+C_{3}\dfrac{1}{N_{s}^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}. (3.1)

Here, 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] denotes the total expectation.

Proof.

See Appendix B. ∎

The bound in Eq. (3.1) shows that Monte Carlo noise yields a residual term of order 𝒪⁡(1/Ns)\mathcal{O}(1/N_{s}). Consequently, the parameter sequence {𝜽k}\{\bm{\theta}_{k}\} converges to an 𝒪⁡(1/Ns)\mathcal{O}(1/N_{s})-neighborhood of a first-order stationary point.

Corollary 3.2.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.2, we have

min1≤k≤K⁡𝔼⁡[‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2]=𝒪⁡(1∑k=1Kηk)+𝒪⁡(1Ns).\min_{1\leq k\leq K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}\right]=\mathcal{O}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(\dfrac{1}{N_{s}}\right).
Remark 3.3.

In contrast to SPRING, the SGD update in VMC admits a conditionally unbiased update direction under Assumption 3.2, enabling first-order convergence results [1]. From this viewpoint, our analysis is closer in spirit to studies that explicitly account for Monte Carlo/MCMC-induced bias in the update direction, such as [19]. The resulting 𝒪⁡(1/Ns)\mathcal{O}(1/N_{s}) residual term is of the same type. We emphasize that (3.1) is an upper bound; in practice, SR preconditioning can yield substantially faster convergence.

A natural question is whether the 𝒪⁡(1/Ns)\mathcal{O}(1/N_{s}) term is merely an artifact of the proof or an intrinsic consequence of stochastic sampling. To investigate this, we conduct numerical experiments on the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising (1D-TFI) model with N=10N=10 sites and transverse-field strength h=1h=1, using a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) ansätz [6] with D=5​ND=5N hidden units (see Appendix D for details). All experiments are implemented using NetKet [34] and JAX [5].

For SPRING, we fix the regularization parameter λ=10−3\lambda=10^{-3} and do not apply the norm-constraint stabilization. Unless otherwise specified, all other algorithmic components follow Algorithm 1. We run SPRING with μ=0\mu=0 and μ=0.99\mu=0.99 under both full-batch evaluation and Monte Carlo sampling with varying sample sizes NsN_{s}. To eliminate MCMC non-stationarity in this experiment, we use direct sampling throughout. For each run, we record the full-batch gradient norm over K=100000K=100000 iterations. The results are reported in Fig. 2.

In this experiment, the full-batch size is 2N=10242^{N}=1024. The results show that, even when NsN_{s} exceeds the full-batch size, stochastic sampling prevents convergence to an exact stationary point. Moreover, the empirical results are well fitted by b/Ns+c/Ns2\sqrt{b/N_{s}+c/N_{s}^{2}}, consistent with the bound in Eq. (3.1). These observations indicate that the 𝒪⁡(1/Ns)\mathcal{O}(1/N_{s}) residual term reflects an intrinsic limitation of stochastic sampling rather than a proof artifact.

3.2 Divergence Counterexample of SPRING with μ=1\mu=1

We now analyze the regime μ=1\mu=1, which exhibits dynamics that are qualitatively different from the case 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1. Throughout this subsection, we focus on the full-batch update (F-SPRING). A key structural property of VMC plays a central role: the gradient g⁡(𝜽)g(\bm{\theta}) always lies in the range of the SR matrix S⁡(𝜽)S(\bm{\theta}).

Lemma 3.3.

Let ℛ⁡(S⁡(𝛉))\mathcal{R}(S(\bm{\theta})) denote the range space of S⁡(𝛉)S(\bm{\theta}). Then g⁡(𝛉)∈ℛ⁡(S⁡(𝛉))g(\bm{\theta})\in\mathcal{R}(S(\bm{\theta})).

Proof.

Denote 𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽))\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta})) the kernel space of S⁡(𝜽)S(\bm{\theta}). For any w∈𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽))w\in\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta})), we have

w⊤​S​(𝜽)​w=𝔼X∼π𝜽​[|O​(𝜽,X)⊤​w|2]=0,w^{\top}S(\bm{\theta})w=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}\left[\left|O(\bm{\theta};X)^{\top}w\right|^{2}\right]=0,

which implies O​(𝜽,X)⊤​w=0O(\bm{\theta};X)^{\top}w=0 π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}}-a.s. Consequently,

g​(𝜽)⊤​w=𝔼X∼π𝜽​[E¯​(𝜽,X)​O​(𝜽,X)⊤​w]=0,∀w∈𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽)).g(\bm{\theta})^{\top}w=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}[\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};X)O(\bm{\theta};X)^{\top}w]=0,\quad\forall~w\in\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta})).

Therefore, g⁡(𝜽)⟂𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽))g(\bm{\theta})\perp\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta})) and hence g⁡(𝜽)∈ℛ⁡(S⁡(𝜽))g(\bm{\theta})\in\mathcal{R}(S(\bm{\theta})). ∎

Remark 3.4.

The same property holds for the Monte Carlo estimators. Indeed, with the usual constructions g⁡(𝛉,ℬ)=2​O​(𝛉,ℬ)​E¯​(𝛉,ℬ)g(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})=2O(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})\bar{E}(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B}) and S⁡(𝛉,ℬ)=O⁡(𝛉,ℬ)​O​(𝛉,ℬ)⊤S(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})=O(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})O(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})^{\top}, we also have g⁡(𝛉,ℬ)∈ℛ⁡(S⁡(𝛉,ℬ))g(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})\in\mathcal{R}(S(\bm{\theta};\mathcal{B})).

Let P𝒦​(𝜽)∈ℝNp×NpP^{\mathcal{K}}(\bm{\theta})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times N_{p}} denote the orthogonal projector onto the kernel space 𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽))\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta})). Projecting the full-batch update (F-SPRING) onto 𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽k))\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta}_{k})) yields

P𝒦​(𝜽k)​Δ​𝜽k=μ​P𝒦​(𝜽k)​Δ​𝜽k−1.P^{\mathcal{K}}(\bm{\theta}_{k})\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\mu P^{\mathcal{K}}(\bm{\theta}_{k})\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}. (3.2)

This identity shows that the kernel component of the update is driven purely by the momentum term. Since both the kernel space and the projector P𝒦​(𝜽k)P^{\mathcal{K}}(\bm{\theta}_{k}) depend on 𝜽k\bm{\theta}_{k}, directly analyzing (3.2) is challenging. To gain intuition, we consider a simplified setting where the SR matrix is fixed.

Heuristic analysis with fixed SR matrix.

Assume S⁡(𝜽)≡S∈ℝNp×NpS(\bm{\theta})\equiv S\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times N_{p}} with 0<rank⁡(S)<Np0<\mathrm{rank}(S)<N_{p}, and let P𝒦P^{\mathcal{K}} denote the associated kernel projector. Then (3.2) reduces to

P𝒦​Δ​𝜽k=μ​P𝒦​Δ​𝜽k−1=⋯=μk​P𝒦​Δ​𝜽0.P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\mu P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}=\cdots=\mu^{k}P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0}. (3.3)

Consequently, the kernel component of the parameter iterate satisfies

P𝒦​𝜽k+1=P𝒦​𝜽0+∑m=0kηm​P𝒦​Δ​𝜽m=P𝒦​𝜽0+(∑m=0kηm​μm)​P𝒦​Δ​𝜽0.P^{\mathcal{K}}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}=P^{\mathcal{K}}\bm{\theta}_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{k}\eta_{m}P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{m}=P^{\mathcal{K}}\bm{\theta}_{0}+\left(\sum_{m=0}^{k}\eta_{m}\mu^{m}\right)P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0}. (3.4)

When 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1, the exponentially decay in (3.3) typically keeps the kernel contribution bounded for standard step-size schedules. In contrast, when μ=1\mu=1, (3.4) becomes

P𝒦​𝜽k+1=P𝒦​𝜽0+(∑m=0kηm)​P𝒦​Δ​𝜽0.P^{\mathcal{K}}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}=P^{\mathcal{K}}\bm{\theta}_{0}+\left(\sum_{m=0}^{k}\eta_{m}\right)P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0}.

If P𝒦​Δ​𝜽0≠0P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0}\neq 0 and the step-size sequence is not summable, the kernel component grows without bound. Since commonly used step-size schedules in VMC satisfy ηk=𝒪⁡(1/k)\eta_{k}=\mathcal{O}(1/k), this heuristic argument explains why μ=1\mu=1 can lead to divergence.

Remark 3.5.

In standard implementations, one often initializes Δ​𝛉−1=0\Delta\bm{\theta}_{-1}=0, so that the first update reduces to an SR step and satisfies

Δ​𝜽0=𝜽1−𝜽0η0=−12​(λ​I+S)−1​g​(𝜽0)⟹P𝒦​Δ​𝜽0=0.\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0}=\dfrac{\bm{\theta}_{1}-\bm{\theta}_{0}}{\eta_{0}}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\lambda I+S\right)^{-1}g(\bm{\theta}_{0})\Longrightarrow~P^{\mathcal{K}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0}=0.

This does not contradict the above mechanism: in practice S⁡(𝛉k)S(\bm{\theta}_{k}) varies with kk, and finite-precision effects can introduce nonzero kernel components after the first iterations. For the heuristic argument, we therefore view 𝛉1\bm{\theta}_{1} as given and analyze the subsequent dynamics of {𝛉k}k≥2\{\bm{\theta}_{k}\}_{k\geq 2}.

More generally, if there exists a subspace

𝒦0⊂⋂k𝒦⁡(S⁡(𝜽k,ℬk)),\mathcal{K}_{0}\subset\bigcap_{k}\mathcal{K}(S(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k})),

then for (SPRING), we can similarly have

P𝒦0​Δ​𝜽k=μk​P𝒦0​Δ​𝜽0,P𝒦0​𝜽k+1=P𝒦0​𝜽0+(∑m=0kηm​μm)​P𝒦0​Δ​𝜽0,P^{\mathcal{K}_{0}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=\mu^{k}P^{\mathcal{K}_{0}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0},\quad P^{\mathcal{K}_{0}}\bm{\theta}_{k+1}=P^{\mathcal{K}_{0}}\bm{\theta}_{0}+\left(\sum_{m=0}^{k}\eta_{m}\mu^{m}\right)P^{\mathcal{K}_{0}}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{0},

where P𝒦0P^{\mathcal{K}_{0}} is the orthogonal projector onto 𝒦0\mathcal{K}_{0}.

Explicit counterexamples.

The heuristic mechanism above can be realized by explicit wavefunction constructions for which the SR matrix is independent of 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Highlight that, under the stochastic setting, the divergence will still happen in some situations.

Continuous example. Consider the Gaussian-type wavefunction on ℝ3​N\mathbb{R}^{3N},

ψ𝜽​(x)=e−14​(x−A​𝜽)⊤​Σ−1​(x−A​𝜽),x∈ℝ3​N,\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(x)=e^{-\frac{1}{4}(x-A\bm{\theta})^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-A\bm{\theta})},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{3N}, (3.5)

∇𝜽​log​ψ𝜽​(𝐱)=12​A⊤​Σ−1​(𝐱−A​𝜽),𝔼X∼π𝜽​[∇𝜽​log​ψ𝜽​(𝐱)]=0.\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2}A^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-A\bm{\theta}),\quad\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}[\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\log\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})]=0.

ψ𝜽(𝐱)=2−N/2e𝐢​𝐱⊤​A​𝜽,𝐱∈{−1,1}N,\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})=2^{-N/2}e^{\mathbf{i}\,\mathbf{x}^{\top}A\bm{\theta}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\{-1,1\}^{N}, (3.6)

Theorem 3.3.

Let {𝛉k}k≥2\{\bm{\theta}_{k}\}_{k\geq 2} be generated by (F-SPRING) or (SPRING) with μ=1\mu=1. Then there exist a wavefunction and an initialization such that

4 PRIME-SR: A Momentum-Adaptive SR Method

In this section, we introduce Principal Range Informed MomEntum SR (PRIME-SR), a tuning-free momentum-adaptive variant of SPRING. The design of PRIME-SR is guided by the theoretical insight from Section 3.2: under aggressive momentum reuse at μ=1\mu=1, instability arises from kernel-related directions. This suggests that momentum control should link to the sampled spectral information revealed by the SR matrix at the current iteration.

Our basic viewpoint is that momentum control should depend on two complementary aspects of the SR information: first, how the sampled spectrum is distributed; second, how reliable the associated sampled directions are. The first aspect is encoded by an effective spectral dimension indicator, while the second is characterized by a subspace-overlap indicator. PRIME-SR combines these two signals to determine the momentum parameter adaptively: stronger momentum reuse is encouraged only when both the spectral and range space information are favorable. Throughout this section, unless stated otherwise, we use the shorthand notations

E¯k:=E¯​(𝜽k,ℬk),Ok:=O⁡(𝜽k,ℬk),Sk:=S⁡(𝜽k,ℬk),gk:=g⁡(𝜽k,ℬk).\bar{E}_{k}:=\bar{E}(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}),\qquad O_{k}:=O(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}),\qquad S_{k}:=S(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}),\qquad g_{k}:=g(\bm{\theta}_{k};\mathcal{B}_{k}).

4.1 Design Principle and Effective Spectral Dimension

We begin with the spectral aspect, and let the SVD of Ok∈ℝNp×NsO_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times N_{s}} be

Ok=[UkℛUk𝒦]​[Σk000]​[(Vkℛ)⊤(Vk𝒦)⊤],Σk=diag⁡(ςk,1,…,ςk,rk),O_{k}=\begin{bmatrix}U_{k}^{\mathcal{R}}&U_{k}^{\mathcal{K}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Sigma_{k}&0\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}(V_{k}^{\mathcal{R}})^{\top}\\ (V_{k}^{\mathcal{K}})^{\top}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\Sigma_{k}=\mathrm{diag}(\varsigma_{k,1},\dots,\varsigma_{k,r_{k}}), (4.1)

where ςk,1,…,ςk,rk>0\varsigma_{k,1},\dots,\varsigma_{k,r_{k}}>0 are the nonzero singular values of OkO_{k}. Therefore, the SR matrix Sk=Ok​Ok⊤S_{k}=O_{k}O_{k}^{\top} has nonzero eigenvalues ςk,12,…,ςk,rk2\varsigma_{k,1}^{2},\dots,\varsigma_{k,r_{k}}^{2}, and rk=rank​(Sk)r_{k}=\text{rank}(S_{k}).

To quantify how the sampled spectrum is distributed, we introduce the following effective spectral dimension:

αk:=(∑i=1rkςk,i2)2∑i=1rkςk,i4≤rk,\alpha_{k}:=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r_{k}}\varsigma_{k,i}^{2}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{r_{k}}\varsigma_{k,i}^{4}}\leq r_{k}, (4.2)

where the upper bound rkr_{k} is from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. This quantity approximately measures the number of principal spectral directions. Indeed, if ςk,12≫ςk,i2\varsigma_{k,1}^{2}\gg\varsigma_{k,i}^{2} for all i≠1i\neq 1, then αk≈1\alpha_{k}\approx 1; if all nonzero singular values are equal, then αk=rk\alpha_{k}=r_{k}. Hence αk\alpha_{k} may be viewed as an effective dimension of the sampled spectrum.

The relevance of αk\alpha_{k} to momentum control is the following. A smaller αk\alpha_{k} means that the sampled spectral information is concentrated on fewer dominant directions, which in turn suggests a potentially larger kernel-related subspace. In this regime, strong momentum reuse carries a higher risk of amplifying unstable components, and the momentum parameter should therefore be reduced. Conversely, a larger αk\alpha_{k} indicates that the sampled spectral information is spread over more effective directions, which is more favorable for aggressive momentum reuse.

Figure 3 illustrates the behavior of αk\alpha_{k} on the 1D-TFI model with N=10N=10, including the full-batch reference and sampled runs with different sample sizes. All other experimental settings are the same as those in Section 3.1. An important empirical observation is that αk\alpha_{k} is relatively insensitive to the sample size and remains close to its full-batch counterpart. This indicates that αk\alpha_{k} stably captures the spectral structure at the current iteration and is therefore suitable as an online stability indicator.

4.2 Subspace Overlap as a Reliability Indicator

The indicator αk\alpha_{k} describes only the sampled spectrum. It does not characterize whether the associated sampled directions are trustworthy. To address this second aspect, we now examine the range space information carried by the singular subspaces of OkO_{k}. From the decomposition in Eq. (4.1), the nonzero spectrum is shared by

Sk=Ok​Ok⊤∈ℝNp×NpandTk=Ok⊤​Ok∈ℝNs×Ns.S_{k}=O_{k}O_{k}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times N_{p}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_{k}=O_{k}^{\top}O_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times N_{s}}.

Meanwhile, the associated range space information is carried by the nonzero left and right singular subspaces:

span⁡(Ukℛ)=ℛ⁡(Sk),span⁡(Vkℛ)=ℛ⁡(Tk).\mathrm{span}(U_{k}^{\mathcal{R}})=\mathcal{R}(S_{k}),\qquad\mathrm{span}(V_{k}^{\mathcal{R}})=\mathcal{R}(T_{k}).

Since αk\alpha_{k} already provides an effective dimension, we define the principal range spaces using the leading ⌈αk⌉\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil directions. Specifically, let Uk,αℛU_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}} and Vk,αℛV_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}} denote the submatrices of UkℛU_{k}^{\mathcal{R}} and VkℛV_{k}^{\mathcal{R}} formed by the leading ⌈αk⌉\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil columns.

The role of subspace overlap is to quantify the reliability of the sampled range space information. Ideally, such reliability should be measured by comparing the effective sampled subspace with the corresponding effective subspace of the true SR matrix S⁡(𝜽k)S(\bm{\theta}_{k}). In other words, the ideal quantity is the overlap between the principal range spaces of SkS_{k} and S⁡(𝜽k)S(\bm{\theta}_{k}). Since S⁡(𝜽k)S(\bm{\theta}_{k}) is unavailable in practice, we introduce two practical surrogates:

  • •

    the left-subspace surrogate, given by the overlap between the principal range spaces of SkS_{k} and Sk−1S_{k-1};

  • •

    the right-subspace surrogate, given by the overlap between the principal range spaces of TkT_{k} and Tk−1T_{k-1}.

These are defined as

βk(U):=‖(Uk,αℛ)⊤​Uk−1,αℛ‖F,βk(V):=‖(Vk,αℛ)⊤​Vk−1,αℛ‖F.\beta_{k}^{(U)}:=\left\|\left(U_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}\right)^{\top}U_{k-1,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}\right\|_{F},\qquad\beta_{k}^{(V)}:=\left\|\left(V_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}\right)^{\top}V_{k-1,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}\right\|_{F}. (4.3)

These quantities measure the overall alignment between the principal sampled directions at two successive iterations. A small overlap indicates that the principal directions extracted from the two sampled matrices differ significantly, suggesting that sampling does not yet stably resolve the underlying effective subspace. By contrast, a large overlap indicates that the dominant sampled directions are consistently identified across iterations, suggesting that sampling is sufficiently informative to capture the underlying effective subspace more reliably. Therefore, larger values of βk(U)\beta_{k}^{(U)} or βk(V)\beta_{k}^{(V)} indicate more reliable sampled directions for momentum reuse.

Figure 4 reports both indicators on the 1D-TFI model with N=10N=10. We observe that both the left- and right-subspace overlaps clearly separate different sample sizes: larger sample sizes lead to larger overlap values. This confirms that both indicators reflect the reliability of sampled range space information.

4.3 Practical Rule and the PRIME-SR Algorithm

Both indicators in Eq. (4.3) are informative, but they differ in computational convenience. The left-subspace overlap is more directly connected to ℛ⁡(Sk)\mathcal{R}(S_{k}). However, computing it requires access to the left singular vectors of OkO_{k}, which is expensive when NpN_{p} is large. We therefore adopt the right-subspace viewpoint and work with the smaller matrix Tk:=Ok⊤​Ok∈ℝNs×NsT_{k}:=O_{k}^{\top}O_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times N_{s}}. Since Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p} in the applications considered here, this choice is substantially more efficient. Accordingly, PRIME-SR uses the right principal-range-space overlap as its practical reliability indicator:

β~k:=‖(Vk,αℛ)⊤​Vk−1,αℛ‖F∈[0,min⁡{⌈αk⌉,⌈αk−1⌉}].\tilde{\beta}_{k}:=\left\|\left(V_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}\right)^{\top}V_{k-1,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}\right\|_{F}\in\left[0,\sqrt{\min\{\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil,\lceil\alpha_{k-1}\rceil\}}\right]. (4.4)

We now combine the two signals into the momentum-control rule. The design principle is simple:

  • •

    a smaller αk\alpha_{k} indicates a potentially larger kernel-related subspace and therefore calls for smaller momentum;

  • •

    a larger β~k\tilde{\beta}_{k} indicates more reliable sampled directions and therefore supports larger momentum.

Hence, the adaptive momentum parameter μk\mu_{k} in PRIME-SR should be increasing in both αk\alpha_{k} and β~k\tilde{\beta}_{k}. We use the following practical rule:

μk:=1−(1−β~kmin⁡{⌈αk⌉,⌈αk−1⌉})​(1−(αkrk)1/4).\mu_{k}:=1-\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{\tilde{\beta}_{k}}{\sqrt{\min\{\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil,\lceil\alpha_{k-1}\rceil\}}}}\right)\left(1-\left(\frac{\alpha_{k}}{r_{k}}\right)^{1/4}\right). (4.5)

The resulting PRIME-SR update is

Δ​𝜽k=−Ok​(λ​I+Ok⊤​Ok)−1​(μk​Ok⊤​Δ​𝜽k−1+E¯k)+μk​Δ​𝜽k−1.\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}=-O_{k}\left(\lambda I+O_{k}^{\top}O_{k}\right)^{-1}\left(\mu_{k}O_{k}^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}+\bar{E}_{k}\right)+\mu_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}. (4.6)

For practical computation, we directly use the spectral decomposition Tk=Vk​Σ~k2​Vk⊤T_{k}=V_{k}\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}^{2}V_{k}^{\top}. Then αk\alpha_{k} admits the equivalent form

αk=(∑i=1rkςk,i2)2∑i=1rkςk,i4=tr​(Σ~k2)2tr⁡(Σ~k4),\alpha_{k}=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r_{k}}\varsigma_{k,i}^{2}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{r_{k}}\varsigma_{k,i}^{4}}=\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}^{2})^{2}}{\mathrm{tr}(\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}^{4})}, (4.7)

so it can be computed directly from the spectrum of TkT_{k}. The matrix Vk,αℛV_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}} is formed by the ⌈αk⌉\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil leading eigenvectors in VkV_{k}, and rkr_{k} is the numerical rank obtained by truncating the spectrum of Σ~k2\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}^{2} using a tolerance εr\varepsilon_{r}. As in our implementation, we use the MATLAB-default choice in rank command: εr=Ns​εm\varepsilon_{r}=N_{s}\varepsilon_{m}, where εm\varepsilon_{m} denotes machine precision.

The additional computational and storage overhead of PRIME-SR relative to SPRING is modest. The extra cost is dominated by the computation of β~k\tilde{\beta}_{k}, which requires 𝒪⁡(Ns​⌈αk⌉​⌈αk−1⌉)\mathcal{O}\left(N_{s}\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil\lceil\alpha_{k-1}\rceil\right) operations per iteration, while the additional storage cost is 𝒪⁡(Ns​⌈αk⌉)\mathcal{O}\left(N_{s}\lceil\alpha_{k}\rceil\right) for storing Vk,αℛV_{k,\alpha}^{\mathcal{R}}. In our experiments, Ns=1000N_{s}=1000 and typically αk≈20∼30\alpha_{k}\approx 20\sim 30, so the overhead is relatively small. Algorithm 2 summarizes PRIME-SR.

Remark 4.1.

At present, the convergence analysis developed in Section 3 does not directly extend to PRIME-SR, since the momentum parameter in PRIME-SR is updated adaptively, whereas our current theory is established for SPRING with a fixed momentum parameter. Nevertheless, the numerical results in the following section show that PRIME-SR provides a clear practical advantage: it substantially improves stability and robustness over fixed-μ\mu SPRING, avoids manual tuning, and achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases better than, the optimally tuned SPRING.

5 Numerical Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the proposed PRIME-SR method and compare it with SPRING using fixed, hand-tuned momentum parameters μ\mu. The goal of these experiments is not to claim uniform superiority over the best fixed choice of μ\mu, but rather to assess whether PRIME-SR can (i) achieve performance comparable to near-optimal fixed-μ\mu SPRING runs, and (ii) provide improved robustness against unstable momentum choices in practical VMC settings.

All experiments are conducted on an Ubuntu 20.04.1 system equipped with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU and CUDA 12.0. Spin-lattice experiments are implemented using NetKet [34], a VMC framework based on JAX [5], while electronic-structure experiments are performed using VMCNet [20].

For spin-lattice models, we consider the TFI model and the Heisenberg model, both with periodic boundary conditions (see Appendix D.3 for details):

  • •

    TFI model

    ℋ=−∑<i,j>σizσjz−h∑jσjx.\mathscr{H}=-\sum_{<i,j>}\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}-h\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}^{x}.
  • •

    Heisenberg model

    ℋ=∑<i,j>σix​σjx+σiy​σjy+σiz​σjz.\mathscr{H}=\sum_{<i,j>}\sigma_{i}^{x}\sigma_{j}^{x}+\sigma_{i}^{y}\sigma_{j}^{y}+\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}.

We test the 1D-Heisenberg model with N=100N=100 sites, and the 2D-Heisenberg and 2D-TFI models with N=10×10N=10\times 10 sites; for the 2D-TFI model we use transverse field strengths h=2,3,4h=2,3,4. These settings follow [3]. For all lattice experiments, we use RBM wavefunction with D=5​ND=5N hidden units, initialized with random seed jax.random.PRNGKey(0) and using 64-bit precision. Each run uses K=10,000K=10{,}000 optimization iterations with Ns=1000N_{s}=1000 MCMC samples per iteration. We employ a burn-in of 30003000 steps, single-spin-flip proposals, and 1010 MCMC transitions between optimization iterations. We apply mean-centered local-energy clipping at 55 standard deviations, following common VMC practice [27, 10]. Reported energy trajectories are smoothed using a sliding window average over 100 iterations, as in [10].

For electronic systems, we consider C\mathrm{C}, N\mathrm{N}, and O\mathrm{O} atoms, as well as LiH\mathrm{LiH}, N2\mathrm{N}_{2} and CO\mathrm{CO} molecules. For N2\mathrm{N}_{2}, we use the equilibrium bond length 2.0162.016 Bohr, and for CO\mathrm{CO} we use 2.1732.173 Bohr, following [10]. Benchmark ground-state energies for C\mathrm{C}, N\mathrm{N}, O\mathrm{O}, N2\mathrm{N}_{2}, and CO\mathrm{CO} are taken from [10], while the benchmark for LiH\mathrm{LiH} is taken from [27]. A standard FermiNet architecture with 16 dense determinants and 32-bit precision is used, consistent with [10]. Each electronic experiment runs for K=100,000K=100{,}000 iterations with Ns=1000N_{s}=1000 samples per iteration. Gaussian all-electron proposals are used, with adaptive standard deviation to maintain an acceptance ratio of approximately 50% (See Appendix D.4 for details). Reported energy trajectories are smoothed using a sliding window average over 3000 iterations.

Across all experiments, we use the inverse-time step-size schedule ηk=η01+c​k\eta_{k}=\dfrac{\eta_{0}}{1+ck} with c=10−4c=10^{-4}. We set η0=0.02\eta_{0}=0.02 for all spin-lattice systems and for C\mathrm{C}, N\mathrm{N}, O\mathrm{O}, and LiH\mathrm{LiH}, and η0=0.002\eta_{0}=0.002 for N​2\mathrm{N}2 and CO\mathrm{CO}, matching [10]. We use regularization λ=10−3\lambda=10^{-3} and a norm constraint C=10−3C=10^{-3} throughout. For fixed-μ\mu SPRING, we tune μ=0,0.2,0.4,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.995\mu=0,0.2,0.4,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.995 for spin-lattice models, and we exclude μ=0.995\mu=0.995 for electronic systems due to stability issues. For PRIME-SR, we set the rank tolerance as εr=Ns​εm\varepsilon_{r}=N_{s}\varepsilon_{m}, where εm\varepsilon_{m} denotes machine precision.

5.1 Experiments on Spin-Lattice Models

Figures 5 and 6 report results for the 2D-TFI model with h=2,3,4h=2,3,4 and for the 1D/2D-Heisenberg models. The corresponding μk\mu_{k} trajectories are plotted every 100 iterations. Across all tested lattice systems, PRIME-SR consistently reaches energy levels comparable to those obtained by the optimal or near-optimal fixed-μ\mu runs. At the same time, the fixed-μ\mu baselines exhibit a clear spread in performance across different choices, indicating that careful tuning is important for obtaining strong results.

Values of μ\mu that perform well on the 2D-TFI problems are not always equally effective on the Heisenberg models, and vice versa. This model dependence makes it difficult to choose a single fixed momentum that works reliably across different systems. In contrast, PRIME-SR remains competitive throughout these tests without requiring problem-specific tuning, which is precisely the practical advantage of the proposed adaptive strategy.

5.2 Sensitivity of Initialization on Electronic Systems

For electronic systems, we observe that fixed-μ\mu SPRING is also sensitive to initialization, i.e., to the initial parameter 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0}, especially for μ≥0.9\mu\geq 0.9. We test five initializations corresponding to random seeds jax.random.PRNGKey(ii) for i=0,1,2,3,4i=0,1,2,3,4. Fig. 7 reports results for N2\mathrm{N}_{2} and CO\mathrm{CO} molecules with μ=0.9,0.95\mu=0.9,0.95. The dependence on initialization is pronounced: for some seeds, the optimization remains stable and reaches low energy error, whereas for others, the same hyperparameter setting leads to visibly worse behavior and can even lead to divergence. This indicates that, in the electronic setting, the performance of fixed-μ\mu SPRING depends not only on the choice of μ\mu, but also strongly on the initialization.

As a direct comparison, Fig. 8 shows the corresponding results of PRIME-SR on the N2\mathrm{N}_{2} and CO\mathrm{CO} molecules across the same set of random seeds. In contrast to fixed-μ\mu SPRING, all runs remain stable and attain similar final accuracies. The reduction in seed sensitivity is one of the main practical advantages of PRIME-SR and highlights its substantially improved robustness in the electronic setting.

5.3 Experiments on Atomic Systems

We next report experiments on the atoms C\mathrm{C}, N\mathrm{N}, and O\mathrm{O}, comparing fixed-μ\mu SPRING and PRIME-SR. Due to instability at large μ\mu, we exclude some μ\mu values from the comparison. Specifically, for C\mathrm{C} atom, we compare against μ=0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99\mu=0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99, while for N\mathrm{N} and O\mathrm{O} atoms we use μ=0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9,0.95\mu=0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9,0.95. Unstable runs for N\mathrm{N} and O\mathrm{O} atoms with μ=0.99\mu=0.99 are reported in Appendix E.1. Figure 9 shows results for random seed 0, and the results of additional seeds are provided in Appendix E.2. The trajectories of μk\mu_{k} are plotted every 1000 iterations.

Across all three atomic systems, PRIME-SR remains stable throughout training and reaches final accuracies that are comparable to the optimal or near-optimal fixed-μ\mu baselines. In particular, it consistently avoids the unstable large μ\mu behavior while retaining the optimization benefits of momentum reuse. Together with the multi-seed results reported in Appendix E, these experiments indicate that PRIME-SR improves robustness to initialization without introducing a noticeable loss in accuracy.

5.4 Experiments on Molecular Systems

We finally consider the LiH\mathrm{LiH}, N2\mathrm{N}_{2}, and CO\mathrm{CO} molecules. We compare against fixed-μ\mu SPRING with μ=0\mu=0, 0.20.2, 0.40.4, 0.60.6, 0.80.8, 0.90.9, 0.950.95, 0.990.99 for LiH\mathrm{LiH} molecular, and μ=0\mu=0, 0.20.2, 0.40.4, 0.60.6, 0.80.8, 0.90.9, 0.950.95 for N2\mathrm{N}_{2} and CO\mathrm{CO} molecules. Unstable runs for N2\mathrm{N}_{2} and CO\mathrm{CO} molecules with μ=0.99\mu=0.99 are reported in Appendix E.1. Figure 10 shows results for random seed 0, and results of additional seeds are reported in Appendix E.3.

The molecular systems show the same overall trend. PRIME-SR remains stable over the full optimization horizon and reaches accuracies comparable to optimal fixed-μ\mu SPRING. For CO\mathrm{CO}, PRIME-SR can even outperform the best stable fixed-μ\mu run in our experiments. The additional multi-seed results in Appendix E further support the conclusion that PRIME-SR provides a more robust alternative to fixed-μ\mu SPRING on molecular problems.

6 Conclusion and Discussion

VMC has become a central tool for studying strongly correlated quantum systems, where the expressiveness of modern neural network wavefunctions must be matched by stable and efficient optimization algorithms. Among existing approaches, SPRING, the momentum-accelerated variant of SR, has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in VMC optimization. However, this strong practical performance relies on carefully tuned momentum parameters, and the stability and convergence behavior of SPRING have remained insufficiently understood.

In this work, we investigated the stability and convergence properties of SPRING for wavefunction optimization in VMC. We provided a theoretical characterization of the role of the momentum parameter μ\mu, showing that the regimes 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1 and μ=1\mu=1 are governed by fundamentally different mechanisms. In particular, we established convergence guarantees for μ<1\mu<1 under mild assumptions, and constructed explicit counterexamples demonstrating that μ=1\mu=1 can induce divergence through uncontrolled growth along kernel-related directions of the SR matrix. Building on these insights and numerical observations, we proposed PRIME-SR, a tuning-free momentum-adaptive SR method that controls momentum reuse through spectral flatness and subspace-overlap indicators derived from the SR matrix. Extensive experiments on spin-lattice systems as well as atomic and molecular electronic systems show that PRIME-SR achieves performance comparable to optimally or near-optimally tuned fixed-μ\mu SPRING while substantially improving robustness.

Several directions for future work remain. From a theoretical perspective, it would be desirable to extend the current analysis beyond idealized sampling assumptions and fixed-μ\mu settings, and to better understand the mechanisms behind the instability occasionally observed in electronic-structure runs even when μ<1\mu<1. Such behavior likely reflects a subtle interplay between sampling noise and SR ill-conditioning, and may also depend on the specific Hamiltonian and wavefunction parameterization. On the algorithmic side, exploring even simpler or theoretically justified indicators of sampling quality or curvature structure could further improve the adaptive mechanism. Finally, the kernel-range viewpoint underlying our design is not specific to SPRING, and similar adaptive principles may be applicable to other SR-based or geometry-aware optimization methods.

To prove Theorem 3.1, we first establish the following lemmas.

Lemma A.1.

‖g⁡(𝜽)‖≤2​Cm,‖S⁡(𝜽)‖2≤Cm.\left\|g(\bm{\theta})\right\|\leq 2\sqrt{C_{m}},\quad\left\|S(\bm{\theta})\right\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{C_{m}}.

Lemma A.2.

Under Assumption 3.1, let {𝛉k}\{\bm{\theta}_{k}\} be generated by (F-SPRING), then for any 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1,

∑k=0∞ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2<∞.\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}<\infty.

g⁡(𝜽k)=2​λ​μ​Δ​𝜽k−1−2​(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k))​Δ​𝜽k,𝜽k+1−𝜽k=ηk​Δ​𝜽k.g(\bm{\theta}_{k})=2\lambda\mu\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}-2(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k}))\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k},\quad\bm{\theta}_{k+1}-\bm{\theta}_{k}=\eta_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}.

And further by 2​Δ​𝜽k⊤​Δ​𝜽k−1=‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2−‖Δ​𝜽k−Δ​𝜽k−1‖22\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}=\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}-\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}, we have

L⁡(𝜽k+1)−L⁡(𝜽k)≤(λ​μ+Cg2​ηk)​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+λ​μ​ηk​(‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2−‖Δ​𝜽k−Δ​𝜽k−1‖2)−2​ηk​Δ​𝜽k⊤​(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k))​Δ​𝜽k≤(λ​μ+Cg2​ηk−2​λ)​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+λ​μ​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2−λ​μ​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−Δ​𝜽k−1‖2.\begin{split}L(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-L(\bm{\theta}_{k})&\leq\left(\lambda\mu+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\eta_{k}\right)\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left(\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}-\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\right)\\ &\quad-2\eta_{k}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}^{\top}\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\\ &\leq\left(\lambda\mu+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\eta_{k}-2\lambda\right)\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}-\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}.\end{split} (A.2)

Consider the discrete energy Fk:=L⁡(𝜽k)+λ​μ​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2≥EGSF_{k}:=L(\bm{\theta}_{k})+\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\geq E_{\text{GS}}, which is bounded from below. Thus, by Eq. (A.2), we have

Fk+1−Fk=L⁡(𝜽k+1)−L⁡(𝜽k)+λ​μ​ηk+1​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2−λ​μ​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2≤(λ​μ+Cg2​ηk−2​λ)​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+λ​μ​ηk+1​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2−λ​μ​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−Δ​𝜽k−1‖2(by ​ηk+1≤ηk​ and ​ηk≤η0)≤(−2​λ​(1−μ)+Cg2​η0)​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2−λ​μ​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−Δ​𝜽k−1‖2<0,\begin{split}F_{k+1}-F_{k}&=L(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-L(\bm{\theta}_{k})+\lambda\mu\eta_{k+1}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}-\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\\ &\leq\left(\lambda\mu+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\eta_{k}-2\lambda\right)\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+\lambda\mu\eta_{k+1}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}-\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\\ &(\text{by }\eta_{k+1}\leq\eta_{k}\text{ and }\eta_{k}\leq\eta_{0})\\ &\leq\left(-2\lambda(1-\mu)+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\eta_{0}\right)\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}-\lambda\mu\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}<0,\end{split}

where the last <0<0 is from the Assumption 3.1 on η0\eta_{0}. Therefore, FkF_{k} decreases monotonically. Assume that limk→∞Fk=F∗\lim_{k\to\infty}F_{k}=F^{*}, then

F∗−F0=∑k=0∞Fk+1−Fk≤(−2​λ​(1−μ)+Cg2​η0)​∑k=0∞ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2−λ​μ​∑k=0∞ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−Δ​𝜽k−1‖2<0.F^{*}-F_{0}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}F_{k+1}-F_{k}\leq\left(-2\lambda(1-\mu)+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\eta_{0}\right)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}-\lambda\mu\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}-\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}<0.

Hence, we obtain ∑k=0∞ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2<∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}<\infty. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Theorem 3.1.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

We first estimate g​(𝜽k)⊤​Δ​𝜽kg(\bm{\theta}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}, from the update in (F-SPRING), we have

g​(𝜽k)⊤​Δ​𝜽k=−12​g​(𝜽k)⊤​(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k))−1​g​(𝜽k)+λ​μ​g​(𝜽k)⊤​(λ​I+S⁡(𝜽k))−1​Δ​𝜽k−1(by ​S​(𝜽k)⪰0​ and from Lemma A.1 ​‖S⁡(𝜽k)‖2≤Cm)≤−12​(λ+Cm)​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2+μ⁡‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖(by Young inequality)≤−12​(λ+Cm)​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2+μ4​(λ+Cm)​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2+μ⁡(λ+Cm)​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2=μ−24​(λ+Cm)​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2+μ⁡(λ+Cm)​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2.\begin{split}g(\bm{\theta}_{k})^{\top}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}&=-\dfrac{1}{2}g(\bm{\theta}_{k})^{\top}\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)^{-1}g(\bm{\theta}_{k})+\lambda\mu g(\bm{\theta}_{k})^{\top}\left(\lambda I+S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right)^{-1}\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\\ &(\text{by }S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\succeq 0\text{ and from \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{lem:g_S_bounded} }\left\|S(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{C_{m}})\\ &\leq-\dfrac{1}{2(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}+\mu\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|\\ &(\text{by Young inequality})\\ &\leq-\dfrac{1}{2(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{\mu}{4(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}+\mu(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}\\ &=\dfrac{\mu-2}{4(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}+\mu(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}.\end{split}

Substituting this inequality into Eq. (A.1), we obtain

L⁡(𝜽k+1)−L⁡(𝜽k)≤μ−24​(λ+Cm)​ηk​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2+μ⁡(λ+Cm)​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2+Cg2​ηk2​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2(by ​ηk≤ηk−1​ and ​ηk≤η0)≤μ−24​(λ+Cm)​ηk​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2+μ⁡(λ+Cm)​ηk−1​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2+Cg​η02​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2.\begin{split}L(\bm{\theta}_{k+1})-L(\bm{\theta}_{k})&\leq\dfrac{\mu-2}{4(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\eta_{k}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}+\mu(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{C_{g}}{2}\eta_{k}^{2}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}\\ &(\text{by }\eta_{k}\leq\eta_{k-1}\text{ and }\eta_{k}\leq\eta_{0})\\ &\leq\dfrac{\mu-2}{4(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\eta_{k}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}+\mu(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})\eta_{k-1}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{C_{g}\eta_{0}}{2}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}.\end{split}

Rearranging the terms, we obtain

2−μ4​(λ+Cm)​ηk​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2≤μ⁡(λ+Cm)​ηk−1​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2+Cg​η02​ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+L⁡(𝜽k)−L⁡(𝜽k−1).\dfrac{2-\mu}{4(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\eta_{k}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}\leq\mu(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})\eta_{k-1}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{C_{g}\eta_{0}}{2}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+L(\bm{\theta}_{k})-L(\bm{\theta}_{k-1}).

Summing from k=1k=1 to k=Kk=K, we obtain

2−μ4​(λ+Cm)​∑k=1Kηk​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2≤μ⁡(λ+Cm)​∑k=1Kηk−1​‖Δ​𝜽k−1‖2+Cg​η02​∑k=1Kηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+L⁡(𝜽1)−L⁡(𝜽K+1)≤(λ​μ+Cm​μ+Cg​η02)​∑k=0∞ηk​‖Δ​𝜽k‖2+L⁡(𝜽1)−EGS<∞.\begin{split}\dfrac{2-\mu}{4(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}&\leq\mu(\lambda+\sqrt{C_{m}})\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k-1}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k-1}\right\|^{2}+\dfrac{C_{g}\eta_{0}}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+L(\bm{\theta}_{1})-L(\bm{\theta}_{K+1})\\ &\leq\left(\lambda\mu+\sqrt{C_{m}}\mu+\dfrac{C_{g}\eta_{0}}{2}\right)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_{k}\left\|\Delta\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\|^{2}+L(\bm{\theta}_{1})-E_{\text{GS}}<\infty.\end{split}

∑k=1Kηk​‖g⁡(𝜽k)‖2≤C.\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}\left\|g(\bm{\theta}_{k})\right\|^{2}\leq C.
